title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
subject: Algorithms & Data Structures
metaphorStory: Imagine an anime courier standing on a twilight hilltop with a glowing lantern. Her mission is to deliver an urgent message to the distant celestial haven (Node G). Rather than recklessly rushing down unknown paths, she projects a radiant beacon across every neighboring junction. At each step, she greedily commits to the path with the smallest cumulative light-distance, permanently locking it in as verified before expanding her aura to the next closest beacon.
academicConcept: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path between nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It maintains a set of visited vertices and a priority queue (min-heap) of tentative distances from the source. At each iteration, the unvisited vertex with the minimum distance is extracted, and the tentative distances of its adjacent neighbors are updated (relaxed). Time complexity with a Fibonacci heap is O(V log V + E) or O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.
keyTakeaways: Greedy Strategy: Always selects the unvisited node with the lowest tentative distance.
Edge Relaxation: If dist[u] + weight(u, v) < dist[v], update dist[v].
Invariant: Once a node is visited/settled, its shortest distance from the source is finalized.
Limitation: Fails with negative edge weights (requires Bellman-Ford instead).

hotspots.label: Source Node (0)
hotspots.explanation: Distance initialized to 0; all other nodes start at infinity (∞).

hotspots.label: Cyan Luminous Edge (Relaxation)
hotspots.explanation: Path A -> C (weight 5) is evaluated. If reaching C through A is faster than alternative paths, C's tentative cost is updated.

hotspots.label: Min-Heap Selection
hotspots.explanation: Out of unvisited nodes, the node with the minimum tentative value is chosen next.

hotspots.label: Destination (G) Shortest Path: 14
hotspots.explanation: The finalized path: Source (0) -> A (5) -> C (8) -> E (11) -> F (13) -> G (14).

visualCueCards.title: The Relaxation Formula
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: Lantern light beam connecting Node U to Node V
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] then dist[v] = dist[u] + w(u, v)
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: Why do we say 'relax' an edge?
visualCueCards.answer: Because we 'loosen' an upper bound on distance, tightening our estimate closer to the true shortest path.

visualCueCards.title: Why Negative Weights Break Dijkstra
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: A dark vortex that steals lantern energy retroactively
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: Dijkstra assumes visited nodes never need distance reduction.
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: What happens if an edge weight is -10?
visualCueCards.answer: A previously finalized node could have its distance reduced by taking the negative edge later, violating the greedy invariant.

visualCueCards.title: Time Complexity Anchor
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: A binary heap tree floating like starlight
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: O((V + E) log V) with Binary Min-Heap
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: Where does the 'log V' factor come from?
visualCueCards.answer: From extracting the minimum element and updating priority queue keys for up to E edges.

activeRecallQuiz.question: If Node C is extracted from the min-heap with distance 8, can any later path reduce C's distance in a graph with all non-negative weights?
options: No, because all remaining paths have at least distance 8 and edge weights cannot be negative.
Yes, if a longer path has more intermediate nodes.
Yes, if the destination node hasn't been visited yet.
Only if the graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Correct! Because all edge weights are >= 0, traversing through any other unvisited node (which already has tentative distance >= 8) can only increase or keep the distance the same.

title: Binary Search Trees, Rotations & Traversals
subject: Data Structures & Tree Algorithms
metaphorTitle: The Celestial Yggdrasil of Balanced Runes
metaphorStory: Imagine an ancient anime scholar atop an observatory tower gazing at the celestial World Tree of Numbers. Every radiant branch obeys the Sacred Rune Law: any rune to the scholar's left must hold a lesser magnitude, while any rune to the right must hold a greater one. When one side grows heavy with star-nodes, the branches perform an ethereal rotational dance (AVL rotation) to restore equilibrium, ensuring knowledge can always be retrieved in O(log N) steps.
academicConcept: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a hierarchical node-based data structure where each node has at most two children. The left subtree contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key, and the right subtree contains only keys greater. Unbalanced BSTs can degenerate into O(N) linked lists, which self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) solve via tree rotations to guarantee O(log N) search, insertion, and deletion.
keyTakeaways: BST Property: Left < Root < Right for every node in the tree.
In-Order Traversal: Visiting Left -> Root -> Right yields elements in strictly sorted ascending order.
Rotations: Left and Right rotations adjust tree balance without violating the BST ordering property.
Height Balance: Keeps max depth at ~1.44 log2(N) in AVL trees, avoiding worst-case O(N) degeneration.

hotspots.label: Root Node (15)
hotspots.explanation: All nodes in the left branch (7, 3, 11) are < 15; all in the right (24, 20, 28) are > 15.

hotspots.label: AVL Rotations (Left & Right)
hotspots.explanation: Single and double rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) rebalance subtrees when height factor difference |H_left - H_right| > 1.

hotspots.label: In-Order Traversal
hotspots.explanation: Traversing Left -> Root -> Right produces: 3, 7, 11, 15, 20, 24, 28 (strictly sorted!).

visualCueCards.title: In-Order Gives Sorted Order
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: A walking beam traveling from lowest leaf to highest leaf
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: In-Order: Left -> Node -> Right = Sorted Sequence
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: Why does in-order guarantee sorted values?
visualCueCards.answer: Because by definition, everything smaller (left) is printed before the node, and everything larger (right) is printed after.

visualCueCards.title: The Single Left Rotation
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: Branch bending like a wind turbine lifting the heavy child up
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: Right-heavy unbalance (RR): Right child becomes new root, old root becomes its left child.
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: What happens to the inner subtree during rotation?
visualCueCards.answer: The new root's left child is reassigned to become the old root's right child, preserving BST invariants.

activeRecallQuiz.question: What is the worst-case search time in an UNBALANCED binary search tree with N elements inserted in strictly ascending order?
options: O(N), because it degenerates into a single long linked-list chain.
O(log N), because binary search always divides in half.
O(1), because the element is at the root.
O(N log N), because of repeated comparisons.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Spot on! Inserting elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in sorted order into an unbalanced tree creates a right-skewed single chain resembling a linked list, requiring O(N) traversals.

title: Operating Systems: Concurrency, Mutex & Deadlock
subject: Systems & Computer Architecture
metaphorTitle: The Twilight Tramway Crossroads & The Circular Gridlock
metaphorStory: Imagine a serene anime mountain train terminal at dusk with glowing celestial tracks. Two historic trams (Thread A and Thread B) need to traverse a single scenic bridge (the Critical Section). To prevent collisions, the station master holds a glowing brass key (the Mutex Lock). Only the tram holding the key can enter the bridge. But if four trams each enter a circular junction, each clutching one section of track while waiting for the next tram to move forward, a permanent twilight freeze occurs: Deadlock!
academicConcept: Concurrency occurs when multiple instruction sequences execute simultaneously (or interleaved) sharing resources. A Critical Section is code accessing shared resources that must not be concurrently executed. A Mutex (Mutual Exclusion) lock guarantees that only one thread executes the critical section at a time. Deadlock occurs when a set of processes are permanently blocked because each holds a resource and waits for another resource held by another process.
keyTakeaways: The 4 Coffman Conditions for Deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.
Deadlock Prevention: Eliminating ANY ONE of the four Coffman conditions guarantees deadlock cannot occur.
Resource Allocation Graph (RAG): A cycle in a RAG with single-unit resources is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
Banker's Algorithm: A deadlock avoidance algorithm that checks for a 'safe state' before allocating resources.

hotspots.label: Critical Section Bridge
hotspots.explanation: Single track where only one tram (thread) is allowed at any moment to prevent race conditions.

hotspots.label: Mutex Lock Key
hotspots.explanation: Acquired before entering the critical section; released immediately upon exit.

hotspots.label: 4 Coffman Conditions
hotspots.explanation: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption, 4. Circular Wait.

hotspots.label: Circular Wait Loop
hotspots.explanation: Tram 1 holds Track A waiting for Track B; Tram 2 holds Track B waiting for Track A. Circular deadlock!

visualCueCards.title: Break Circular Wait to Prevent Deadlock
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: Numbering all train tracks with glowing hieroglyphs
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: Resource Ordering: Always request locks in strictly increasing numerical order.
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: Why does strict lock ordering prevent circular wait?
visualCueCards.answer: Because a cycle requires at least one thread to hold a higher lock while requesting a lower lock, which the protocol forbids.

visualCueCards.title: Race Condition Mnemonic
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: Two conductor stamps hitting the same ticket at once causing ink smear
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: Outcome depends on uncontrollable thread scheduling order.
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: How do atomic operations solve race conditions?
visualCueCards.answer: They execute as an indivisible hardware instruction that cannot be interrupted by another thread.

activeRecallQuiz.question: Which of the following strategies successfully prevents deadlock by breaking the 'Hold and Wait' condition?
options: Require processes to request and receive all needed resources at once before execution begins.
Allow the operating system to forcefully take resources away from running processes.
Impose a strict linear ordering on all resource acquisition.
Replace all mutual exclusion locks with spinlocks.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Correct! If a process must allocate all resources simultaneously before starting, it never 'holds' some resources while 'waiting' for others.

title: Neural Networks, Forward & Backpropagation
subject: Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence
metaphorTitle: The Celestial Observatory of Starlight Gradients
metaphorStory: Imagine an anime astronomy student standing atop an ancient hillside observatory at sunset. Starlight from distant constellations filters through luminous glass lens layers (Input, Hidden, and Output). At first, the projected star coordinates on her chart are blurry and misaligned (High Initial Loss). By looking backwards through the lens array, she measures the gradient of the blur (Chain Rule Error Derivative) and gently turns the brass dial rings (Weights) step-by-step down the mountain slope until the image snaps into crystalline focus at the Global Minimum.
academicConcept: An Artificial Neural Network computes a prediction through Forward Propagation: linear combinations z = Wx + b passed through non-linear activation functions h = f(z). The Loss Function L(y_hat, y) measures prediction error. Backpropagation uses the Calculus Chain Rule to compute the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each weight (∂L/∂W), and Gradient Descent updates weights in the opposite direction: W := W - η ∇L.
keyTakeaways: Forward Pass: Computes activations layer-by-layer from input to output.
Loss Calculation: Quantifies divergence between prediction and ground-truth target.
Backward Pass (Chain Rule): Propagates error backwards, calculating ∂L/∂w_ij.
Learning Rate (η): Controls the step size down the gradient slope. Too large causes divergence; too small causes slow convergence.

hotspots.label: Input Layer (Features)
hotspots.explanation: Nodes representing raw feature vectors fed into the network.

hotspots.label: Hidden Layers (Representations)
hotspots.explanation: Neurons apply activation functions (e.g. ReLU, GELU) to model non-linear boundaries.

hotspots.label: Loss Curve & Gradient Descent
hotspots.explanation: Loss decreases over iterations towards a local or global minimum via W := W - η ∇Loss.

visualCueCards.title: The Weight Update Rule
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: Stepping down a glowing dusk hillside toward the valley
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: Why the minus sign in the update rule?
visualCueCards.answer: Because the gradient points in the direction of steepest INCREASE; we subtract it to descend toward the minimum.

visualCueCards.title: Why Non-Linear Activations Matter
visualCueCards.visualAnchor: A curved prism bending linear light into complex spectra
visualCueCards.formulaOrFact: Without activations: W2 * (W1 * x) = (W2 * W1) * x = W_combined * x
visualCueCards.intuitionQuestion: What happens if all activation functions are linear f(x) = x?
visualCueCards.answer: No matter how many layers the network has, it collapses into a single-layer linear model unable to learn non-linear patterns.

activeRecallQuiz.question: In backpropagation, which mathematical principle is applied to compute the gradient across multiple connected layers?
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Exactly! The Chain Rule allows us to decompose the composite derivative ∂Loss/∂W through intermediate activations and layer pre-activations.
